title: Why does a microwave have a turntable?

sources.name: Whirlpool engineering patent — Microwave oven switching between predefined modes (2010), background

practice: Try the Science Quiz for more explanations hiding in everyday life.

sections.html:
A microwave turntable rotates the food to help reduce uneven heating. The microwave field inside the oven can have stronger and weaker spots. Moving the food through different positions helps reduce their effect.

Whirlpool's engineering description explains this familiar solution and its limit: a turntable does not produce perfectly uniform heating. The soup gets a ride, but that is not the whole cooking job.
sections.title: A small turn helps with uneven heating

sections.html:
Has the plate ever turned the other way? GE says its turntables can normally rotate in either direction.

They do not have to alternate between starts. For those models, a change of direction is ordinary behaviour, rather than evidence that dinner has confused the machine.
sections.title: Clockwise is not a special ingredient

sections.html:
A visible spinning plate is not compulsory in every design. Panasonic describes a hidden antenna beneath the floor of its NN-SF57RM flatbed model, which rotates microwave energy around the food.

That is one example of a different arrangement. It does not mean every flatbed microwave uses exactly the same system.
sections.title: Some ovens move the energy instead

sections.html:
The plate carries the container around; it does not mix what is inside. Panasonic's cooking guidance still calls for stirring, following food instructions and allowing the specified standing time so heat can spread.

That little rotating stage helps, but the food's instructions still matter. For another clever household mechanism, discover how a toilet flushes without electricity.
